variants.title: Follow the late event
variants.context: A late event is placed by its event time, arrives after the watermark has already published the window, is accepted while the allowed lateness has not expired, corrects the existing result through keyed state, and survives replay because the sink upserts and side effects carry stable keys.
variants.prompt: A ten second order count window covers 10:00:00 through 10:00:10 with 30 seconds of allowed lateness. Put the life of one late order in order.

items.text: Replay reapplies the event, state returns to 127, and the alert's effect key prevents a second page.
Keyed state adds the order and the sink upserts key orders:10:00:00 with the value 127.
The order is created at 10:00:04, so its event time places it in the 10:00:00 window.
The event arrives at 10:00:20, late but still inside the allowed lateness.
The processor crashes before the next checkpoint, so recovery restores checkpoint 841 at offset 2048 with 126.
The watermark reaches 10:00:15 and the window emits a count of 126.

variants.hint: The window publishes once and then gets corrected, rather than waiting forever.
variants.explanation: Late firings are corrections to an existing result, and replay reproduces the same correction because the sink upserts one key.

variants.title: Follow the late event
variants.context: A late event is placed by its event time, arrives after the watermark has already published the window, is accepted while the allowed lateness has not expired, corrects the existing result through keyed state, and survives replay because the sink upserts and side effects carry stable keys.
variants.prompt: A payment lands long after its window closed and after the allowed lateness expired. Put the events in order.

items.text: The watermark passes the window end plus the allowed lateness, so the correction state is dropped.
The payment finally arrives, past the too late boundary.
The payment's event time of 08:00:03 places it in the 08:00:00 window.
The declared policy routes it to a reviewable side output and leaves the published value unchanged.
The watermark passes the window end and the window publishes its result.

variants.hint: Correction state cannot be kept forever.
variants.explanation: Once the watermark passes the lateness boundary the window's state is released, so a later arrival follows the declared too late policy.

variants.title: Follow the late event
variants.context: A late event is placed by its event time, arrives after the watermark has already published the window, is accepted while the allowed lateness has not expired, corrects the existing result through keyed state, and survives replay because the sink upserts and side effects carry stable keys.
variants.prompt: A network retry publishes the same order event twice. Put the handling in order.

items.text: Deduplication state recognizes the event id it has already applied.
The window aggregate is left unchanged instead of counting the order twice.
The downstream write reuses the same effect key, so no second side effect is committed.
The retry publishes the same stable event id a second time to the durable log.
The processor reads both copies from the partition in offset order.

variants.hint: Where can the duplicate still be caught after the aggregate is right?
variants.explanation: Stable event and effect keys stop a duplicate twice, once in the aggregate and once at the business effect.

variants.title: Trace the streaming path
variants.context: The streaming path runs from a producer that stamps stable ids and event times, through a durable partitioned log, into a processor that assigns watermarks and checkpoints its state with input positions, out to feature, analytical, and decision consumers.
variants.prompt: A normal event flows from a checkout service to a fraud decision. Put the path in order.

items.text: The online feature store publishes the versioned, timestamped feature values.
The checkpoint stores that state together with the input positions needed for recovery.
The decision consumer applies an idempotent action and records the outcome join key.
The producer stamps a stable event id, event timestamp, schema version, and source metadata.
The durable log orders the event within its partition and retains it for replay.
The processor validates the schema, assigns a watermark, and updates window and join state.

variants.hint: Which hop makes replay possible at all?
variants.explanation: The durable log and the checkpointed offsets are what let every later stage be recomputed rather than trusted once.

variants.title: Trace the streaming path
variants.context: The streaming path runs from a producer that stamps stable ids and event times, through a durable partitioned log, into a processor that assigns watermarks and checkpoints its state with input positions, out to feature, analytical, and decision consumers.
variants.prompt: The model service starts timing out while events keep arriving. Put what a well isolated pipeline does in order.

items.text: The decision consumer serves a declared fallback and records the degraded state with the join key.
The processor keeps updating windows, joins, and checkpointed state on schedule.
The feature store keeps publishing fresh, versioned feature values for later readers.
The scoring call fails inside its bounded deadline instead of blocking the pipeline.
The producer keeps publishing events with their ids and timestamps.
The durable log retains everything, so nothing is lost while the model is sick.

variants.hint: Which parts of the pipeline have no dependency on the model at all?
variants.explanation: Durable event and feature processing continue through a model outage, and only the decision layer degrades or abstains.

variants.title: Trace the streaming path
variants.context: The streaming path runs from a producer that stamps stable ids and event times, through a durable partitioned log, into a processor that assigns watermarks and checkpoints its state with input positions, out to feature, analytical, and decision consumers.
variants.prompt: A traffic spike pushes publish rates to five times normal. Put the overload response in order.

items.text: The processor caps its queues and state rather than growing memory without limit.
The decision consumer returns a freshness labeled degraded result rather than a stale one presented as fresh.
The producer publishes the burst with stable ids and event timestamps.
The durable log absorbs the burst and applies bounded producer and consumer backpressure.
Lower priority work is slowed, shed, or diverted before memory is exhausted.
Events that keep failing are diverted to a reviewable dead letter path instead of retried forever.

variants.hint: Shedding is a decision, so it needs an order of preference.
variants.explanation: Backpressure slows, sheds, or diverts lower priority work before memory is exhausted, and poison events leave the retry loop.

variants.title: Do the lateness math
variants.context: Allowed lateness is measured from the end of the window, not from its start. A late event is accepted while the watermark has not passed the window end plus the allowed lateness, and after that boundary the declared too late policy applies.
variants.prompt: A ten second window starts at 10:00:00 and the pipeline allows 30 seconds of lateness. How many seconds after 10:00:00 does that window stop accepting corrections?
variants.hint: Allowed lateness starts counting where the window ends.
variants.explanation: The window ends at 10:00:10 and 30 seconds of lateness carry it to 10:00:40, which is 40 seconds after the window start.

mistakes.feedback: That adds the lateness to the window start; the budget begins at the window end.
That is the window end, which ignores the allowed lateness entirely.

variants.title: Do the lateness math
variants.context: Allowed lateness is measured from the end of the window, not from its start. A late event is accepted while the watermark has not passed the window end plus the allowed lateness, and after that boundary the declared too late policy applies.
variants.prompt: A five minute window ends at 12:05:00 with two minutes of allowed lateness. The watermark now shows 12:06:20. How many more seconds may a late event for that window still be accepted?
variants.hint: Part of the budget has already been spent.
variants.explanation: The boundary is 12:07:00 and the watermark has reached 12:06:20, so 40 seconds of the two minute budget remain.

mistakes.feedback: That is the full lateness budget and ignores the 80 seconds the watermark already consumed.
That is the time elapsed since the window end, not the time remaining.

variants.title: Do the lateness math
variants.context: Allowed lateness is measured from the end of the window, not from its start. A late event is accepted while the watermark has not passed the window end plus the allowed lateness, and after that boundary the declared too late policy applies.
variants.prompt: A window ends at 09:30:00 with 30 seconds of allowed lateness. An event for that window arrives at 09:30:45. By how many seconds did it miss the correction boundary?
variants.hint: Find the boundary first, then measure from it.
variants.explanation: The boundary is 09:30:30 and the event arrived at 09:30:45, so it missed by 15 seconds and follows the too late policy.

mistakes.feedback: That is the delay after the window end, not the amount by which the boundary was missed.
That adds the lateness to the arrival delay instead of subtracting the budget from it.

variants.title: Keep replay from changing the result
variants.context: Exactly once is an end to end property. A framework checkpoint replays input, so duplicate business effects are prevented only when the sink upserts by key, participates transactionally, or deduplicates on a stable effect key.
variants.prompt: Checkpointing is enabled, yet every restart leaves extra rows in the analytical sink. What explains it?
options: The sink appends blindly, so replayed events are written again as new rows.
The checkpoint interval is too long, so more events are replayed each time.
The watermark is too aggressive, so windows publish before they are complete.
optionFeedback: A checkpoint replays input, and only an upsert or transactional sink turns that into one result.
A longer interval replays more events, but a correct sink still ends at one row per key.
Watermark aggressiveness changes completeness, not the number of rows written.
variants.hint: Exactly once is a property of the whole path, not of the framework.
variants.explanation: Replay is expected, so the sink has to upsert by key, participate transactionally, or deduplicate for the result to stay correct.

variants.title: Keep replay from changing the result
variants.context: Exactly once is an end to end property. A framework checkpoint replays input, so duplicate business effects are prevented only when the sink upserts by key, participates transactionally, or deduplicates on a stable effect key.
variants.prompt: A late correction also opens an operator alert. After a crash and replay, the on call engineer is paged twice for the same correction. What is missing?
options: A stable effect key for the alert write, checked before committing it.
A longer allowed lateness so the correction does not fire twice.
A retry limit on the alert delivery so the second page is dropped.
optionFeedback: A unique effect key lets replay find the alert already committed and skip it.
Lateness controls which events are accepted, not whether an effect repeats.
A retry limit caps delivery attempts but does not identify the duplicate effect.
variants.hint: What would tell the alert path that this exact effect already happened?
variants.explanation: Business effects are deduplicated on stable keys, because the pipeline will replay the event that produced them.

variants.title: Keep replay from changing the result
variants.context: Exactly once is an end to end property. A framework checkpoint replays input, so duplicate business effects are prevented only when the sink upserts by key, participates transactionally, or deduplicates on a stable effect key.
variants.prompt: An event arrives for a window whose watermark already passed the lateness boundary. What should the pipeline do?
options: Drop it silently, since the window has already been finalized.
Send it to a reviewable side output and leave the published value unchanged.
Reopen the window state and correct the published value anyway.
optionFeedback: Silent loss removes the evidence that the lateness policy is set wrong.
The too late policy is declared in advance and keeps the event visible for review.
The correction state was released at the boundary, so reopening it is not available.
variants.hint: A finalized value and a discarded event are two different decisions.
variants.explanation: Past the boundary the declared policy applies, and a reviewable side output keeps the mistuned lateness visible.

variants.title: Name the semantic
variants.context: Four semantics decide correctness: event time assigns an event to the right period, the watermark says how complete event time progress is, checkpointed state makes a restart reproducible, and idempotent effects make retries safe.
variants.prompt: Match each streaming semantic to what it decides.

pairs.label: Event time
pairs.detail: Which real world period an event belongs to, regardless of when it was processed.

pairs.label: Watermark
pairs.detail: How complete event time progress is, and therefore how long to wait for stragglers.

pairs.label: State and checkpoint
pairs.detail: Whether a restart can reproduce aggregates from the same input positions.

pairs.label: Idempotent effect
pairs.detail: Whether a retry or replay can repeat a business action.

variants.hint: Two of these are about time and two are about recovery.
variants.explanation: Each semantic owns a different failure, so a correct pipeline has to answer all four rather than choosing one.

variants.title: Name the semantic
variants.context: Four semantics decide correctness: event time assigns an event to the right period, the watermark says how complete event time progress is, checkpointed state makes a restart reproducible, and idempotent effects make retries safe.
variants.prompt: Four production symptoms are reported. Match each to the semantic that was wrong.

pairs.label: Event time
pairs.detail: Orders created at 10:00:04 were counted in the minute that began at 10:00:20.

pairs.label: Watermark
pairs.detail: Dashboards lag by four minutes because windows wait far longer than the product needs.

pairs.label: State and checkpoint
pairs.detail: A replacement processor resumed with correct aggregates but the wrong input offset.

pairs.label: Idempotent effect
pairs.detail: A retried refund was written to the ledger twice.

variants.hint: Ask which contract each symptom breaks.
variants.explanation: Misplaced periods, waiting policy, recovery consistency, and duplicate effects are four separate defects with four separate fixes.

variants.title: Name the semantic
variants.context: Four semantics decide correctness: event time assigns an event to the right period, the watermark says how complete event time progress is, checkpointed state makes a restart reproducible, and idempotent effects make retries safe.
variants.prompt: A design review raises four questions. Match each to the semantic that answers it.

pairs.label: Event time
pairs.detail: A backfill replayed today must still land in yesterday's windows.

pairs.label: Watermark
pairs.detail: The team must choose how long to wait for stragglers before publishing a result.

pairs.label: State and checkpoint
pairs.detail: A new processor must resume with the same aggregates and the same input positions.

pairs.label: Idempotent effect
pairs.detail: A payment capture must be safe to send again after a timeout.

variants.hint: Backfills and restarts stress different guarantees.
variants.explanation: Choosing the semantics up front is what makes replay, restart, and correction produce the same answer as the first run.
